The story is a cohesive, well-crafted slice-of-life narrative where every detail contributes to the central theme and climax. The opening establishes the bleak, aging, and unprofitable nature of the Elbe ferry (the cold, the creaking gate, the meager three passengers bringing in just a few euros) as well as Ilse's deep connection to this routine and her late husband, Henning (the empty tobacco tin kept for three years). The interaction with the woman in the trench coat subtly introduces the clash between the modern, fast-paced world and the slow reality of the river. All of these elements naturally build to the climax: the phone call from Jonas (likely her son in Munich) wanting to discuss the poor third-quarter balance and a real estate agent. Because the story has already shown us how deeply ingrained Ilse is in this life—and how unprofitable it actually is—her silent decision to ignore the call and keep her hand on the lever feels completely earned, unified, and satisfying.
